Learning Objectives
Identify resident cell types in normal synovium and their functions.
Identify the main components of synovial fluid and their functions.
Assess the contribution of synovium to common joint arthritides, such as rheumatoid arthritis,
reactive arthritis (Reiter syndrome), primary (idiopathic) osteoarthritis, and posttraumatic
osteoarthritis.
Understand crosstalk modalities and mechanisms involving bone, cartilage, and synovium
within the synovial joints.

Overview
Synovial joints are specialized structures that allow movement at bony articulations.
Synovial joints are composed of a joint cavity lined with synovium, containing bones lined with
articular cartilage.
Joints are stabilized by ligaments, whereas joint motion occurs via tendon attachments from
adjacent musculature.
Formation and Development
Formation and development of synovial joints is poorly understood.1
Limb skeletogenesis begins with long, uninterrupted condensations of mesenchymal tissue.
Condensations of mesenchymal cells form at specific locations. This process appears to be
controlled by the homeobox family of genes.
Apoptosis then occurs within the so-called interzone, and the tissues separate via cavitation.
Joint-specific development then ensues via a control mechanism not yet understood.
Structure
The anatomy of each joint varies according to the location and demands of motion placed on
the joint. Joint structure ranges from highly matched bony surfaces, such as the ball-and-
socket hip joint, to the less congruent shoulder joint, which allows greater range of motion but
with less inherent stability.2
Structural components
Articular cartilage—Relatively avascular tissue, populated by chondrocytes, that is specialized
to enable low-friction movement. Extracellular matrix is rich in type II collagen and sulfated
glycosaminoglycans.3,4
Ligament—Collagenous structure connecting articulating bones; provides stability and
restraint to non-physiologic motion
Joint capsule—Tough, fibrous tissue surrounding the joint cavity
Synovium—Tissue that lines the non-cartilaginous portions of the joint cavity; composed of
two layers, the intimal lining and the connective tissue sublining2,5,6
The intimal lining is a few cells thick, is in direct contact with the joint cavity, and produces
synovial fluid. It functions as a porous barrier, lacks tight junctions between cells, and has
no true basement membrane.

The relatively acellular sub-lining is composed of fibroblasts, fat, blood vessels, and
lymphoid cells. A rich vascular network supplies the sub-lining and enables the high solute
and gas exchange that supplies the cartilage with nutrition.
The subintimal synovial membrane has three distinct tissue morphologies.
Areolar: loosely organized collagenous tissue
Adipose: fatty tissue similar in structure to intra-articular fat pads
Dense: dense collagenous tissue
Synovial lining cells are predominantly two lineages in the healthy joint.
Fibroblast-like synoviocytes (type B cells)—Cells of mesenchymal origin that secrete the
hyaluronan and lubricin components of synovial fluid
Macrophages (type A cells)—Cells of a hematopoietic lineage that account for
approximately 25% of the resident cells of the synovium and are responsible for
phagocytosing particles from synovial fluid
Synovial fluid
An ultrafiltrate of plasma with a low albumin concentration (45% compared with plasma)
and a high concentration of hyaluronic acid and lubricin (proteoglycan 4)
Synovial fluid is imbibed and exuded by articular cartilage and other intra-articular soft-
tissue structures as a function of mechanical loading. Clearance from the joint is achieved
via local lymphatic vessels.
Synovial fluid provides gas exchange and metabolic support for chondrocytes within the
relatively avascular articular cartilage.
Shock absorption and lubrication of the joint are from hyaluronic acid and lubricin
(proteoglycan 4).
Lubricin is responsible for boundary lubrication at the articular cartilage surfaces to
minimize friction during movement.
Hyaluronic acid provides a shock-absorbing effect within the joint by imparting viscosity
and other non-Newtonian fluid properties to the synovial fluid.
Loss of hyaluronic acid molecular weight is associated with advancement of joint disease
and degeneration.
Viscosupplementation aims to temporarily replace the loss of higher molecular-weight
hyaluronic acid.
Cells found within synovial fluid
Under normal (non-pathologic) scenarios, synovial fluid may contain synoviocytes shed
from the synovial membrane and a relatively small number (<100 per mL) of leukocytes
(usually monocytes).

Inflammatory conditions, joint trauma, and joint infection may lead to an influx of
lymphoid cells, including polymorphonuclear neutrophils, T lymphocytes, B lymphocytes,
and mast cells. These may be incidentally found in synovial fluid aspirate, but typically
these cells infiltrate the synovium.
Synovial fluid also may contain microscale and nanoscale calcium phosphate particles,
especially in the presence of specific types of joint pathologies.7
Calcium pyrophosphate: calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (also known as
pseudogout)
Calcium oxalate: hyperoxaluria
Monosodium urate: gout
Basic calcium phosphate: end-stage osteoarthritis
Innervation of synovial joints
Fast-conducting myelinated type Aß fibers, which are found in the joint capsule, ligaments,
menisci, surrounding musculature, and local periosteum, produce information on joint
positions and motion (proprioception). Proprioception is derived from feedback from
Pacinian corpuscles and Ruffini endings that terminate these type Aß fibers.
Unmyelinated type Ad and C fibers are found in bundles along blood vessels (sympathetic
nerve fibers) in the capsule and synovium. These fibers transmit diffuse pain sensations and
contribute to vasodilation/vasoconstriction in proximal vasculature.
The Hilton law states that joints are innervated by branches of the same nerves that supply
the muscles responsible for moving the joint.
The Gardner observation states that the portion of the joint capsule that becomes tightened
by a specific muscle group contraction receives its innervation from the same nerves that
supply the antagonizing muscle group, which establishes local reflex arcs that aid in joint
stability.
Synovial Joint Arthritides
Rheumatoid arthritis—Autoimmune condition resulting in cartilaginous and bony erosion
within affected joints. The fibroblast-like synoviocytes biology becomes pathologic;
hyperplastic synovium leads to pannus formation, in which extensions of the synovium
infiltrate subchondral bone; and inflammatory cells and T lymphocytes are recruited. Serology
demonstrates the presence of rheumatoid factor and anti-citrullinated protein antibody, with
elevation of acute phase reactants (erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein level)
during active disease according to the 2010 American College of Rheumatology/European

League Against Rheumatism guidelines.8 Joint involvement usually is symmetric and
polyarticular and frequently includes small joints.9
Reactive arthritis (Reiter syndrome)—Postinfectious arthritis most often associated with a
gastrointestinal (campylobacter, salmonella), sexually transmitted (Chlamydia trachomatis), or
other (group A Streptococcus) infection. The synovial membrane becomes inflamed and
produces large amounts of proinflammatory cytokines. Patients are rheumatoid factor
negative, but the condition is linked to human leukocyte antigen B27.
Primary (idiopathic) osteoarthritis—Most common form of osteoarthritis observed clinically.
The synovium becomes inflamed and hyperplastic postinjury, producing large amounts of
proinflammatory cytokines and matrix-degrading enzymes. The joint degeneration pattern is
classically referred to as wear and tear, but numerous clinical phenotypes with unique
patterns of degeneration and symptomatology have been characterized. Some variants of
osteoarthritis are associated with genetic predisposition. Dissimilar from rheumatoid arthritis,
osteoarthritis is nonerosive and is more commonly observed in large joints, but it also is
frequently observed in small joints of the hand.
Posttraumatic osteoarthritis10—Joint degeneration attributable to a specific instance of joint
trauma. Mechanisms of injury include but are not limited to intra-articular fracture,
ligamentous disruption, and chondral injury. Posttraumatic osteoarthritis most commonly
occurs in the ankle and knee, followed by the hips. Degeneration is rapidly progressive, with
patients requiring joint replacement at a much younger age than their counterparts with
idiopathic osteoarthritis.
Benign Disorders of the Synovial Membrane
Pigmented villonodular synovitis is a benign proliferative condition that primarily affects the
synovium of joints.13 It is characterized by the proliferation of synovial tissue and deposition of
hemosiderin within the synovial membrane. In patients with pigmented villonodular synovitis,
the synovial membrane demonstrates numerous villi and nodules and may be focal or diffuse.
Patients often have insidious onset of pain, swelling, stiffness, and catching of the joint11,12
(Video 1)
Synovial chondromatosis is a condition characterized by the formation of cartilaginous
nodules within the synovium. These nodules may become loose bodies within the joint and
undergo mineralization. This condition is most common in the knee, hip, elbow, and shoulder.
It can occur as a primary condition and secondary to idiopathic osteoarthritis.

Synovial hemangioma is a rare condition consisting of a localized or diffuse vascular
malformation of the synovial membrane. It can occur as an isolated condition or as part of
systemic disease (eg, von Hippel–Lindau syndrome). Recurrent hemarthrosis is commonly
observed, and patients have long-standing pain, swelling, and limited range of motion.

Joint Cross Talk Among Bone, Synovium, and Articular Cartilage
Substantial communication occurs between tissues of the synovial joint, primarily in
development and pathologic processes. Remodeling of subchondral bone appears to be linked
to alterations in articular cartilage and inflammation within the synovial membrane.
Researchers are beginning to more thoroughly define these cross-tissue relationships and the
mechanisms underlying their direct and indirect communication in response to growth,
trauma, and acute or chronic immune actions. A more thorough understanding of the cross-
tissue communication responsible for healthy joint homeostasis may lead to the development
of pharmacologic strategies to prevent and/or manage joint arthritides.6

Synovium-cartilage cross talk
Cartilage is a relatively avascular tissue and receives much of its nutrition from synovial
vasculature and metabolites located within synovial fluid. Similarly, paracrine signaling
from fibroblast-like synoviocytes and macrophages may lead to an influx of chemokines,
cytokines, and matrix-degrading enzymes, which subsequently bathe the articular cartilage
in a proinflammatory and degenerative synovial microenvironment.
After joint trauma, such as anterior cruciate ligament rupture, the synovium produces large
amounts of matrix-degrading proteases, including matrix metalloproteinases 2 and 3.
Substantial increases in proinflammatory cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor alpha
and inteleukin-1 beta from synovium, further bathe the articular cartilage in a degradative
milieu in the posttraumatic setting.
Synovium-bone cross talk
The bulk of communication between synovium and bone is in the form of paracrine
signaling; however, end-stage arthritic disease may lead to pannus formation.
An inflammatory response within the synovium, whether from trauma or systemic
inflammatory disease, may drive synovial macrophages to differentiate and adopt an
osteoclastic phenotype, which may promote the resorption of subchondral bone.
Inflammatory signaling from the synovium also recruits monocytes to the affected joint, the
location at which they undergo osteoclastic differentiation and activation of their resorptive
capacity.
Synovial signaling also drives articular cartilage changes, which directly affect the
underlying subchondral and epiphyseal bone.
Cartilage-bone cross talk
Given the direct contact between articular cartilage and subchondral bone, communication
between these tissues is obvious. Pore networks at the cartilage-bone interface facilitate
solute transport between the two tissues.
In advanced stages of idiopathic osteoarthritis, loss of articular cartilage thickness often
corresponds with thickening and a sclerotic appearance of the subchondral bone (cortical)
plate.
The relationship between articular cartilage thickness and subchondral bone thickening is
less clearly established. Joint trauma may result in a loss of subchondral bone plate
thickness that resembles disuse osteopenia; however, it may be more closely related to the
increased rate of remodeling observed during the subacute phase. Joint trauma also may
induce pathologic focal thickening of articular cartilage in the acute and midterm phase.
Focally thickened cartilage often is hypercellular and stains intensely for sulfated

glycosaminoglycans; however, it has a fibrillated and fissured articular surface that
underlies the poor mechanical properties of this reactive tissue. Regional thickening of
articular cartilage after joint trauma may be the result of osmotic swelling, focal increases
in extracellular matrix production by chondrocytes, or a combination of both.14
The trabecular network of epiphyseal bone deep to the subchondral bone plate also
undergoes morphologic changes in patients with idiopathic osteoarthritis and
posttraumatic osteoarthritis. During the acute and midterm phases, this trabecular
network demonstrates increased catabolism, manifested as a reduction in trabecular
thickness and trabecular number, with a concomitant increase in trabecular spacing. As
chronicity increases, the anabolism of the trabecular bone network may have transient
increases; however, a steady loss in epiphyseal bone trabecular architecture and density
that may underlie the development of microfractures and marrow lesions closer to the
subchondral bone plate has been demonstrated in more advanced stages of joint disease.
Differences in clinical characterization methods, in addition to poor phenotypic
characterization of osteoarthritis, may contribute to contrasting reports of the temporal
relationships between thickening or thinning of articular cartilage and subsequent
subchondral and epiphyseal bone changes.
